utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 2nd of June. I would like to greet Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Stojic, as well as Mr. Praljak. I would like to greet all the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his associates, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I would first of all like to give the floor to our Registrar, who has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Praljak Defence has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness Slobodan Praljak. The list will be given Exhibit IC1024. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. The Trial Chamber will hand out an oral decision relating to the behaviour of the parties. I shall read it out slowly. The Trial Chamber was informed that after the hearing of the 28th of May, 2009, Mr. Stringer and Mr. Karnavas had quarrelled inside the courtroom. The Trial Chamber cannot ignore this fact, in the presence of people who may have been shocked by this kind of behaviour; quite legitimately so. The Trial Chamber would, therefore, like to ask Mr. Stringer and Mr. Karnavas to apologise in public, and remind them that whatever the circumstances may be, they must, in light of their positions, behave in a dignified manner and in control. In addition, the Trial Chamber has noticed that on several occasions Mr. Karnavas behaved before the Chamber in a way which the Trial Chamber cannot accept. The Trial Chamber would like to recall at the hearing of the 26th of May, 2009, Mr. Karnavas overtly criticised, and in no uncertain terms, the position adopted by the Trial Chamber when it ruled on the closed session which had been asked. Mr. Karnavas said he was quite shocked by the decision that had been handed down by the Trial Chamber; see the transcript on pages 14.755 in private session. Let me correct the page number. It's 40.755. The Trial Chamber would also like to recall that at the hearing of the 28th of May, 2009, Mr. Karnavas' behaviour was totally out of proportion and quite shocking when he addressed Mr. Stringer to say they had not received the e-mail for Mr. Prlic; refer to transcript number 40.965 and subsequent pages. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber has noticed that Mr. Karnavas' tone is totally out of place. This has to do not only what he says in the courtroom, but the Trial Chamber would also like to refer to the tone of voice adopted by Prlic's Defence in its submissions, when it says request filed by Jadranko Prlic with a view to re-examining the decision on the request filed by the Prlic Defence to have documentary evidence admitted into evidence; filed confidentially on the 8th of May, 2009. By way of illustration, the Trial Chamber refers Mr. Karnavas to paragraph 12 of his submission, in which he exposes the reasons why he feels that the Trial Chamber lacks an insight. The Trial Chamber would also like to note that Mr. Karnavas has already been asked to comply with adequate rules of behaviour. This was mentioned on the 3rd of February, 2009. He was sanctioned pursuant to Rule 46(A)(1) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and an oral decision was handed down by the Trial Chamber on the 14th of January, 2009. The Trial Chamber, therefore, asks Mr. Karnavas to submit his views before the 4th of June, 2009, on the behaviour that has been mentioned above so that the Trial Chamber can, if need be, take appropriate measures. There are two important things regarding this oral decision: A, what happened at the end of last week, which opposed Mr. Stringer to Mr. Karnavas when the Trial Chamber had already left the courtroom. The Trial Chamber would, therefore, like to ask both protagonists to apologise. The Trial Chamber realises that Mr. Karnavas is not here today, but he will do so when he comes back, and, therefore, ask Mr. Stringer to apologise to the Chamber. In addition, the Trial Chamber would like to ask Mr. Karnavas, who's not here today, but his co-counsel will inform him about this, we would like to have his remarks put down in writing on what the Trial Chamber has just mentioned in its oral decision, relying on a series of facts, as it did so. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and to everyone else in and around the courtroom. I've heard what the Trial Chamber has said. The events that you've described, Mr. President, that occurred on the record from last week don't require any comment from me. I think the Trial Chamber has made its observations about that. What happened -- I can tell the Trial Chamber what happened after the proceeding ended. I approached Mr. Karnavas in the courtroom. I said things to him that were better left unsaid or probably could have been better said to me -- by me to him alone and not in the presence of the court staff, co-counsel for the other accused. And if I said anything or acted in a way that was offensive or troubling to anyone else, I sincerely apologise for that, and I do wish to apologise to the Trial Chamber for what occurred after the proceedings. We do get riled up at times, as you know, in this court, and I've tried very hard, in the time I've been involved in this trial, not to do that and to stay in control of myself, my temper; and I think I've, for the most part, been able to do that pretty well. But I did lose a bit of self-control and should not have approached Mr. Karnavas in the presence of everyone else in the way I did, and again I apologise to anyone who was present who may have been offended or troubled by that, and I wish to apologise to the Trial Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, this is now on the record. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you for your words. The Trial Chamber would, therefore, like to ask the co-counsel to inform Mr. Karnavas of this decision so that we receive his submissions before the 4th of June. Mr. Praljak, your in-chief will resume, and I would therefore, to this effect, give the floor to Ms. Pinter again, whom I greet this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar just told me that one of the Defence counsel would like to address the Trial Chamber for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. I just wanted to notify the Chamber that regarding the documents that the Trial Chamber has asked me to deliver - actually, it was last week - that a motion would be filed either this evening or, at the latest, tomorrow morning. These are just technical matters regarding translation and so on, so I think that you will receive it by e-mail tomorrow morning at the latest. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us continue with the binder entitled "The Main Staff." Could you please look at document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you explain about the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, the general has just reminded me we have been obliged by His Honour Judge Antonetti to provide notice regarding documents pertaining to May 1993 and Mostar. What we have managed to ascertain so far is that the documents bearing number 01, the documents issued by -- documents issued by the commander, but it might also occur that Mr. Raguz was also issuing documents bearing this designation, 01. He was in charge of relations with UNPROFOR at the time. Documents bearing the reference number beginning with 03 are documents that are issued by the operations office of the Command, and by analysing documents through e-court, it has been a ascertained that these are the reports that are sent to the Main Staff about daily developments in Mostar. As regards the other task that we received, and that was to notify the Trial Chamber about the documents that are or are not in e-court, I can say that General Praljak's Defence has up-loaded into e-court all the documents it had as of the 1st -- or, rather, from the 1st until the 15th or the 16th of May, 1993. And having gone through the e-court, we have also ascertained that the Prosecution also has the same documents. So these are the documents that are at our disposal. They were -- they have been presented, and some, indeed, have been admitted into evidence, either as Prosecution or as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will have ample opportunity to address these issues again when I shall put my questions to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more -- just one brief notice. Some of these documents are in the binder pertaining to Mostar 1993, but not all of them, because we selected only those that have not yet been admitted and that might be of some use to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So, General, I would like you to look at document 3D01097. It has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that was sent using packet radio, so there can't be my signature on it, but it is a document I issued. And here, once again -- well, it deals with the fact that at that time, when the BH Army had launched an extremely strong attack on Bugojno, and from Bugojno towards Gornji Vakuf, simply the whole system broke down. In other words, the units were disjointed. They were not carrying out their orders, and simply -- well, in a military it's ridiculous to write words to the effect of "last warning because of the failure to carry out orders," because you could use wording like that in education, but not in military. But, unfortunately, we had to issue such threats several times and beg and show that our lack of power, in a way, by issuing such orders, in order to organise those exhausted units, disorganized units in some way in order to mount a defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to open document 3D01101. It's yet another order that you issued.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same sort. The date is the 25th of July, and the attacks are really fierce. Our lines in the area of Gornji Vakuf are in disarray, for all intents and purposes, and I add here that at that time in particular -- with many, but in particular there were problems with the units from Livno, for a very simple reason, because they were under strong influence of their local authorities, and Mr. Stanko Vrgoc and Mr. Andabak sometimes - and we'll see later - to put it quite simply, did not obey orders, and here in the PS, I actually threaten them; although if you were to ask me what I had to threaten them with, I would be hard-pressed to give you an answer. Because if you issue a threat, then usually you have to be able to back it with something, some sanctions, and you have to have a way to implement them. But at that point in time, unfortunately, we did not have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you told us that you had read a lot of things. You quoted us a lot of books about the war. Perhaps you read books about World War I. During World War I, there were, in the French forces, some units that did not abide by the orders. These people were court-martialed and executed as a result. Didn't you read anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have read a lot. For instance, the Russian Red Army, just behind the fighters that were mounting an assault, there were the NKVD people who would simply shoot on the spot anyone who attempted to run away or run back. So there's a lot of such instances in the wars; not only in the First World War, in any war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I have to follow up with a question. And what was the situation like in the HZ-HB and the HVO? Why did you not have this procedure in place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Pinter, you will see later on that we did instigate proceedings and that -- well, first of all, the Main Staff was not able to remove a brigade commander easily. It was a long, drawn procedure. There would be a report first and so on. Only Mate Boban was in a position to do so. So you file a report, and by the time it reaches Mr. Boban, who's probably away attending some talks and so on, so it was a long road. And there is also a question of how to investigate the whole matter. There was a commission that was supposed to be set up to determine the facts and so on. And at the time when the fate -- or, rather, there was the problem of the BH Army breaking through the lines. It had to be resolved within a day or two or even a couple of hours. Simply, well, we did carry out those things. Sometimes I did demand that somebody be removed from their posts. I used all kinds of means, threats and other acts. And, on the other hand, if a unit refuses to obey an order, together with its commander, then in the kind of organisation that existed in the HZ-HB, you really don't know what to do with this unit. Naturally, you should have to have a military court and stiff sanctions, but down there, although we did do this, you will see the number of proceedings that were instituted, but it was impossible to achieve this kind of a solid organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like you to look at document 3D01908 -- 019088. I don't think that I gave the correct number. I think it should be 01988, 3D.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an excellent commander from Tomislavgrad, Zeljko Glasinovic, who was a professional soldier. He took part in an operation that NATO launched to liberate Kuwait. He was a professional soldier. He served in the Canadian Army, and his nickname was Glava. And that's why I say "Glava" here, using his nickname, and I tell him, Well, I'm not going to issue any orders to you. I simply expect you to join the fight because the situation is very serious, too serious for any stories and for fucking around. That's what it says here. Well, this is a document -- Your Honours, you know, the worst thing is when you realise, and a commander must not really allow himself to do that, when a commander realises that an order would not be obeyed, it's better not to issue any orders, because then the order would not be obeyed, and you destroyed what little authority you have in front of those people. Of course, you have some authority vis-a-vis the people that are fighting. So it's better not to issue an order, because the whole system breaks down when people see that an order has not been obeyed, and it is also -- it also becomes quite obvious that you don't know what to do, in terms of sanctions, because you are severely limited, and then it’s better to count on people’s willingness to do things; in other words, you're a soldier, you are aware of the situation, I'm not going to order you anything. I'm just expecting you to do something. And this tells you what situation we faced and what the level of organisation was in that army; although I keep repeating that one should differentiate between those who fought honorably and obeyed orders and those who didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please look at P03719. This is a response to a memo signed by Tihomir Blaskic or, rather, somebody signing it for --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document dated -- well, here Mr. Blaskic is responding to the commander of the Nikola Subic Zrinski Brigade from Busovaca. And it would take us a long time to comment on it. The document speaks for itself in terms of what kind of control Mr. Blaskic had when he -- well, this commander from Busovaca, the commander of this brigade, is subordinated to Mr. Blaskic, and something of this sort does not exist in an organised army. This is the kind of correspondence providing some explanations. This would be more fit for diplomacy or some civilian structure, where two people haggle over who understood what in what way and who should do something. It's not a situation where you have a commander who issues an order that had to be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But could you please look at item 6 and 7, in particular 7, in this response, where he informs the commander of his duties.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And who is in charge of the displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he tells him that in socialism, there was the council of workers in companies, and in the self-management system that existed in Yugoslavia, they actually made decisions. It was the highest-ranking organ in a factory or any kind of company, and all first decisions were debated there. I remember in school the council of workers would discuss whether one would buy Grundig or Siemens Electronics, and carpenters, janitors, and cleaning ladies took part in the debate, on an equal footing. So Tihomir Blaskic says, You have to exercise command and control and leave the refugees to the civilian bodies. But it's easy to say that, but when you have displaced persons in Prozor who have come from Bugojno - we said that there were 15.000 of them - then it's easy to say it's for the civilian authorities to deal with. But if you see that the civilian authorities cannot do it, then you can't just leave them there and not get involved, not help them. It is simply just shifting responsibility, and I didn't act in this way. And if the civilian authorities need something, and at the same time you see that they cannot do what they are supposed to do; so you have to assist in the effort to take care of the 15.000 people, to find buses to transport them wherever, to coal, get the oil for the gasoline for the buses, introduce some kind of order and so on. So, in other words, if you see that there's a problem, and you have a responsibility as a human being, regardless of your structural responsibility, it has always been my attitude that you have to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, if I look at this passage on item 7, it seems to me almost a caricature, because here is Colonel Blaskic writing a long letter, discussing with a subordinate commander this and that, and then he puts in "your responsibility is to pass decisions by issuing orders." I think he's right, but what kind of example is he giving? Isn't that a contradiction in terms or at least the behaviour of a chief which by his superior ought to have been corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I'm not sure I understand what the contradiction is about. It must be the translation or something. I'm sorry. I just don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would not exclude that it is my mistake. I don't like having everything blamed on our poor and valiant interpreters. What I mean is this: On the one hand, we have here a two-page - three-page in the translation - letter of a military commander to his subordinate in which he discusses, in a very civilian tone, like in an administration of social welfare organisation or something like that. He discusses this problem with his subordinate as if they were having a glass together. And in the framework of this, however, he tells his subordinate, You must order. You must decide and pass orders. He, himself, is not doing this, he is discussing; and how can he expect the subordinate to act as a military commander when he, himself, acts like a talk-master of some sorts? And the ultimate question is: Wouldn't it have been for the commander of Mr. Blaskic to tell him to comply with what he demands of his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Blaskic did issue an order to him, but he did not comply with this order. Blaskic had received military training on the hands of the JNA, whereas the Busovaca commander probably hadn't, and those who hadn't were thick on the ground. So the first thing he's telling him is this: I remember how it worked with Blaskic, and I remember this one document. It said, I order that yesterday's order that I had issued be carried out. That was the general tone, the same as the threats that I used to make. Just go ahead and try not carrying out this order, if you dare. And they don't, but then what can you do? There's a brigade there with a single commander appointed by someone, or rather you have to select a different mode of communication, and then he tries and explains to him what he has to do in order to become a commander because there's nothing he can do about him. I can make threats to the effect that I'll beat someone up, or star [as interpreted] someone; but the simple fact of the matter is this is a failure to carry out orders. So this is the case, and you can't replace a brigade commander, and you can't throw half the brigade into jail. Well, then, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Praljak, in fact I have read the letter by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. I don't have much problem with it, inasmuch as, if I take your own testimony into account, when you said that this was an army just being formed, not like any other army, so I can understand that the commander somehow teaches, trains his subordinate by way of this rather lengthy letter. However, I think that this commander is right. In item 2, when he says this, when he addresses the issue of a commander's responsibility, he sets out a theory of military command and the commander's responsibility. With regard to this opinion expressed by Colonel Blaskic, it seems to be opposed to yours. Yours is that in a situation characterized by chaos, in a psychological situation of generalised revenge, it was impossible to supervise what your subordinates were doing, but this does not seem to be Colonel Blaskic's theory. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at paragraph 2, Your Honour Judge Mindua, Blaskic says that if there is someone in Busovaca not carrying out orders, he says, this has to be prosecuted. And one has to be very determined about this. If you take measures against those failing to carry out orders, in that case, he addresses the brigade commander, instructing him thus: It is not up to you to liberally discuss this. Try to distinguish between soldiers, on the one hand, and civilians, and the commander as well, the army distinguish, because they are responsible, regardless of the zone. And I don't see here Blaskic is teaching him how that should work. Nevertheless, again and again I have stated and restated this in this courtroom, everyone simply knows what should be done. That is terrifyingly simple. What should an army look like? What should a court look like in Bosnia-Herzegovina? It's very simple when it's written down on paper. But the question that follows is: How does one actually do this on the ground in a situation where there is fighting going on and you are facing problems with people who are there - I have to say this again - of their own free will. Yes, there has been a mobilisation, but the essence of this mobilisation is this: If you fail to respond, then you go to jail for 20 or 30 years, in countries such as France, or America, or elsewhere. If you have a mobilisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, be it for Bosnians, for Muslims, or for Croats, they can all go where they please, but what happens to you is you lose any legal basis whatsoever to do anything else. Any soldier can come up to you and tell you, Throw me in jail, if you like, and then once I'm out of jail, I'll jut cross the border, and that's that. And then you have nothing up your sleeve. You have nothing to threaten them with, except to try and talk them into it. So it turns into more of a conversation trying to convince them, persuasion. You yell at them, you shout at them. I had the ability to do that to a far greater extent than Blaskic. Blaskic was more of a soldier. I was a soldier, too, but I had other methods available to me to motivate people, to praise them, to threaten them, to punish them. It's an entirely different perspective, the army, on the one hand, and in Rama -- or Prozor in July, for example, you had 15.000 persons, and 1.500 soldiers had lost the will to fight in any way whatsoever. And there is nothing at all you can do to make them fight again. All they want to do is go to Croatia because in their own native area they had lost everything by this point. This is a huge crowd of people no longer organised in any way whatsoever. There is no will left in their eyes. There is no tenacity. They have no motive to fight on. They have no desire to fight on. Regrettably, you have no legal basis to do anything about this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us move on to 3D01527.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order that I wrote. This is the situation on the 28th and over the following period. The situation wasn't entirely bad. As far as the army was concerned, I was the commander, the commander of the Main Staff. In the simplest of terms, I refused to lose this war. The chief duty of any commander in any army is not to lose in a battle or war. At this point in time, for me, it was important not to lose Gornji Vakuf or Rama, so what I'm doing here is I'm mobilising all civilian police officers into HVO units, and I am making threats to the effect that I would beat them black and blue or have them shot, which was an exaggeration, needless to say. But the circumstances too were excessive, exaggerated. Obviously, the shooting would not have occurred, needless to say. It's just a threat that I'm making here in a bid to convey this to the civilian police officers, and making a threat to the effect that I would have them shot. And it's absolutely true, Your Honours, that as far as this document on mobilisation was concerned, I'm not sure if I had a legal basis to actually pass anything like this, in terms of sending civilian policemen to the front-line. But at the moment, they, too, were part of the armed forces, and they were armed; whereas I had no intention of losing out. I'd lost Bugojno, but I refused to lose Vakuf and all the rest because these forces that were attacking us at the time were on their way to, as they said, sweep everything clear all the way up to Croatia's border. And I certainly didn't need any sweeping cleared by the BH Army. I was no occupier in those parts. A year or so before, we had fought alongside each other against Republika Srpska. It's true that I'd made these threats, but that's all they were, empty threats, of course. You see, Your Honour Judge Mindua, once you've scared someone like this, then you go and have a talk in Travnik, such as the one you saw in the other document. You try to raise their morale, you try to talk to them, tell them what would happen; that there would be refugees, that they would be expelled, and so on and so forth. So much for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: P03778, please. Thank you. This has been exhibited already. Nevertheless, we have discussed the topic covered by this document a great deal already, so perhaps you, General, should now explain what it is about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived down there on the 24th. I talked to General Petkovic, and we assessed the situation. We ascertained that in a military sense, the situation was more than bad. My decision was to go to the Uskoplje-Rama front. All of our assessments told us that this would be an axis -- strategic axis used by the BH Army in order to push through. If we lost that, it would be difficult to stop them anywhere else. I then asked to have military police placed under my command as an operative unit, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Done by who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban and Mr. Bruno Stojic, the co-signatory. Mate Boban made the call, but the first person I went to was Mr. Stojic and Mr. Boban. The decision, nevertheless, was eventually taken by Mate Boban. Stojic was there to operationalise this decision. Nevertheless, one thing that is noteworthy here is that Mr. Coric's understanding is correct as to what this operative subordination would mean, how it would work. He says that in addition to the military involvement of these units mentioned here, and they're being subordinated to the HVO, one needed to make sure that there would be lasting functional links between the military police units as well as links back to the Military Police Administration. They remained a separate organisation, which at one point in time, and for the purpose of certain missions - this was very specific in terms of time and space - they were subordinated for particular missions to me for the sake of fighting, in an operative sense. And then I dispatched them to certain areas based on my own assessments or perhaps those made by Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have just seen two documents that are interesting if they are compared with one another. I have a question in this respect. In the first document, you, yourself, issue an order to mobilise the civilian police from Tomislavgrad, for those meant to be sent to combat. If I'm not mistaken, there were 5.000 inhabitants in that municipality -- in the town, and the municipality had 30.000 inhabitants. If you take out members of the civilian police to send to the front-line, how is public order to be secured if there are no more members of the civilian police? And in the order that you signed, you don't say anything about this. However, in the second document signed by Mr. Coric, it shows that, unlike you, he recalls that the military police, of course, can be found on the front-line and in fighting, but has to carry on with its ordinary tasks. I have a very specific question here. When you issue an order to take out civilian police for the men to be in two fighting forces, how do you ensure public order and security, because that is an open door for theft, for robbery, attacks and such-like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that's right, but it wasn't Tomislavgrad; it was Rama, Prozor. And over in Prozor, there were no more than 1.500 to 2.000 persons remaining in the town itself. I don't know about the surrounding villages. It is true that my decision would reduce the general security, but you have to bear in mind that at this point in time, my own lines had been broken through, and my assessment at the time was there was no security at all, to speak of, especially if the BH Army managed to get into Rama and do the same thing they had done in Bugojno. Therefore, it is true that this was a reduction in security. How exactly it worked with the military police, well, that's another matter altogether, but in principle I'm aware of that. And when I make this decision, I'm fully conscious of that. Defence is uppermost, it's the uppermost mission and task. After the defence, there is nothing more to be sorted out there if people leave as they did in Bugojno, and then the whole of Vakuf and Rama head for Croatia. This is something they did in France, because what was there to defend in France when the Germans were there and they started restoring their own kind of order. For example, Judge Antonetti, the very famous example, when the Americans got three or four of the major gangsters, such as Lansky and others, to keep watch over the New York harbours because with their own organisation, they were powerless to do anything about the Germans sinking Queen Elizabeth II in the New York harbour. And they got Lansky and Giuliano and all the other gangsters on the job. You used to keep watch over this area before, so you'll do the same thing throughout the war. That's what they told me -- that's what they told them. My lines had been broken through. I was aware in danger of losing territory. And when I made this decision, I was perfectly conscious of the danger that you have just addressed. But, nevertheless, this does not in any way mean that if someone committed a crime because of this, because they thought that they were amnesty. There was still time to track them down to prosecute them. Even 30 or 50 years later, there would be time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 3D02425. It's the daily intelligence report. I'm just saying that for the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says, for Prozor, that operations in Doljani, Pisvir --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 29th of July. At that time, there was major fighting in that area, at least from the perspective of our war. I don't know, of course -- well, these are not movements of units such as the ones you see in the great wars, but people are getting killed. And what would happen to us would be that the commanders from the BH Army because, unfortunately, the lines were not covered as they should be covered in a way, that they would infiltrate our area and were able to capture civilians, soldiers, weapons. And I speak about the developments here. We managed to recapture some of the territory, re-establish some of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In Doljani?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Doljani, Pisvir, in this whole area. Well, in Bugojno there was some fighting still going on. In the hotel, there was a group. They were later killed, but most people actually committed suicide; HVO soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at the Operation Zone South-East Herzegovina. This is a report from the VOS about the intentions of Arif Pasalic and his 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this document, 2D2425 [as interpreted] is a daily report from the Military Intelligence Service, reporting to the authorities, that is, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, reporting to them what's happening on the ground for the various sectors; Tomislavgrad, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Central Bosnia, and South-West Herzegovina. I don't know whether there were similar reports for Mostar, but if I assume that prior to the 9th of May, the military intelligence services more or less knew what the ABiH were doing, there should be this kind of report, and these reports could show us that the ABiH was preparing an attack on Mostar. What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, it is highly likely that they do exist. I can look, although, as I've already said at that time I was not -- I did not receive those reports because I did not have any official capacity. I did not receive the reports that were addressed to the Main Staff, but I know that this gentleman was very much "au courant" with what was happening among it's Muslims and the Republika Srpska troops and that he wrote those reports quite regularly. And it is quite logical to assume that he should speak about how much they knew about the preparations on their part, because it -- well, there were always such communications in such places, and the BH Army was preparing for an attack because they did draft plans. And if an army drafts plans, quite enough people know about that for the other side to learn of it. It was very difficult to keep things confidential because the people talked too much about those things and secrets could not be kept for a long time, in particular when it came to an attack of this kind. We can look for it . JUDGE ANTONETTI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I would like you to look at page 2. I'm really being persistent here about the dispatching of BH Army soldiers to the area, to South-East Herzegovina, Bijelo Polje, Dreznica, and so on. Were you aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were preparing for it. Later on -- and even before Neretva-93, that offensive. Well, it didn't start then. There were constant reconnaissance missions and preparations. So we were aware of their activities much earlier than was officially confirmed, and even before the offensive continued towards south, especially on the 13th of August when they struck on us south of Mostar, near Buna and Blagaj, where they took possession of some elevations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And was this linked with Mostar, was it close to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's all close to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So they were able to reach Mostar. Very well. Now I would like you to look at document 3829.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, no. I'm sorry, we did not get the answer to my question. Line 16, I said: "So they were able to reach Mostar?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. So the document is P3829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, General Praljak. I mean, everything goes so fast that we really need to scrutinise every document. And as I discover them at the last minute, I'm a bit slow to react. I'm very sorry for this, so I ask you this somewhat belatedly. It's because I've just discovered this document. Allow me to ask you to return to the last paragraph in this document. I'm under the impression that the Military Intelligence Service is saying that Pasalic and the 4th Corps had contacts at the highest level, so it seems, with the Serbs in order to, as it were, crucify or harm the HVO, or crush the HVO. And if I try to understand what is said, I understand that the lines of communication were supervised, were monitored, be it on the tactical levels or other levels. Since you came into office for the highest responsibility of the HVO in July, what did you know? Did the Military Intelligence Service have any means of listening in to the enemy in order to hear what the enemy was preparing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the answer is yes, but not so well that you could have the kind of surveillance that is meant when you say "surveillance" today, when you can hear everything being said even through a window. Now, as an engineer, I can tell you that it is impossible for you to talk to somebody and for that conversation not to be monitored if somebody really wants to monitor it. There are technical means to do that. But what I wanted to tell you is because of the way this war was waged and the civilization that existed in this area, when Mr. Pasalic went to talk to the Serbs, and you have seen this from the documents that I tendered, Drekovic and what he says, that for a long time they did not have any military lines proper, only sentinels facing the Serbs. And Sejtanic who writes in his book, "We continue our good cooperation. We agreed about artillery support," and all this goes to show - this is why I tender this into evidence - that there was constant -- well, at one point it began, and it might be June or July 1993, there was constant cooperation between the two armies against the HVO. And here in Mostar, in East Mostar, it is impossible for Pasalic and Orucevic to go and talk to the Serbs without it becoming public knowledge. And then it was always relayed to us, to Mr. Keza, at least, because Mr. Keza was highly competent. He had his people, and his connections, and then it would get relayed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it seems, on the basis of several documents we've seen, that there were contacts between the Serbs and the ABiH. We listened carefully to the sniping events described in Mostar. We listened carefully to your version of the events. Let me remind you of this. I stand to be corrected if I make a mistake. You said that the shots came from the Muslim areas, and perhaps even from the Serb areas, denying that the shots could have come from the HVO. If I adopt your version, i.e., that shots might have come from the Serb side, how can you explain, then, that the Serbs and the Muslims got on, nonetheless the Serbs shot at the Muslims? How can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very simple, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. I analysed the sniping incidents that were analysed here by the expert, and I was able to ascertain that very accurately. And I will get back to it, that as far as Brkica Street is concerned, there is no line of sight from the HVO. So from the HVO-controlled areas, there is no line of sight. It is impossible to wound those two men from their positions, or the child that was wounded in the front, in the direction in which it was running, and so on. So I can't say -- I did not say that nobody fired any shots from the HVO at anyone with 100 percent certainty, but Serbs and Muslims did not become friends. Serbs, the Republika Srpska Army, for their own reasons, very clear reasons, provided support to the BH Army in order -- provided artillery support, sold them weapons, in order for them to defeat the HVO. And from the talks and the agreement that was signed in September, Muslims would get a piece of Bosnia with their majority, and Serbs would take their part with them to Serbia. The objective is very clear and visible from the September agreement Alija Izetbegovic reached with Karadzic and others. And had they managed to achieve that, I claim, no matter what other people might think, that the international community would confirm that, would accept that as a fait accompli just to end the war. There were no principles at play here, as far as I know, but that's why Serbs were assisting them. But it didn't prevent them from firing on the Muslims at the same time and then blaming it on the HVO, to keep the war escalating. I can only tell you that in Capljina, that was controlled by the HVO, so to speak, in 1992, I was shot at from behind, from an area. A burst of gun-fire around my feet. Fortunately, I was not hit. And I know that snipers were active from various apartments in Capljina, and I ordered that all the blinds be pulled down. And I said that if blinds are not pulled down, you can just fire on that window, regardless of the fact that it was summer, because people were left behind, snipers, and they fired at will, killed people, just as they did in Sarajevo. And I will not now claim who those people are, but that was not HVO, because the HVO did not have any reason to do so. But as far as the HVO -- as far as the sniper incidents that I analysed are concerned, I will go through them. The house at Stotina, which is exposed to artillery fire from BH Army positions, well, it cannot be used, Your Honours, as a house. Well, the house that is so weak that a round fired from an anti-aircraft machine-gun would fire it from, well, you cannot have a sniper being active from that house because a round from this anti-aircraft gun would simply blow this house apart. So I cannot rule out the possibility that somebody fired shots from someplace, but no fact that was presented to us by the expert was actually correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The document is P3829. It is your notification or order or a comment. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 30th of July, it obviously happened that some military police units brought into custody some drivers who were driving German humanitarian aid and beat those people up and stole the vehicles. So they were out of control. And I am writing to the head of the Defence Department and to Boban, and that's for their information. And I am ordering Mr. Valentin Coric to put them in jail. This is for him to act, for his action. And this document shows that I'm completely mad. You can call me the furious Orlando, as Torquato Tasso described him, as you can see from these documents. So I'm really furious, completely furious because you have to impose order, and the question is how to do it. And I want him to tell me what prison they were in. There's no reason for me to comment on these documents, because I think they speak for themselves about the state of mind and the situation that prevailed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Praljak, were they actually brought before you, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, to be perfectly honest, I don't know. I can't remember right now, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was running from one front-line to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You don't have to justify. It's absolutely credible, and I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D01986, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is this your document, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there. This document, too, shows what I was asked about by the Trial Chamber. Again, I am requesting the multiple rocket-launcher from a brigade commander from Livno. According to the logic of war, there is nothing for him to consider or think about here. If I send in a request for that multiple rocket-launcher - and again I'm stating here that I had requested one already - the 31st was perhaps the worst day. The night before, the entire front-line held by the HVO in Gornji Vakuf had fallen. So again I am making a threat here. I'm threatening Commander Vrgoc, who couldn't care less about me as some -- he's just not interested in this order, so I'm threatening him here that he would be removed and made to answer under all the military laws. Again, I don't know when this man was eventually replaced. It did take a long time, but he was not prosecuted at all, because I don't know what laws we could possibly have used to prosecute him. Under those same laws, probably 30 or 40 or 50.000 persons should have been prosecuted, if laws like that had existed. All the more, I respected even more those who obeyed and who fought and who were carrying out orders. Vrgoc simply failed to carry out these orders. It was very difficult for me. If I had actually had time to go there and see him, I would have beaten him to a pulp, Your Honours, just to make that perfectly clear. But I simply did not have the time because probably they would have brought me before a Court for that, because I had done that to him. So things being what they were, at this point in time, this was all I could do, no more than this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to wait for the transcript. That's why I'm pausing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have noted what you've just said. You needed this 125-millimetre multiple rocket-launcher, and you asked the Kresimir Petar Brigade, the 4th Brigade in Livno, to provide you with this. The commander of this brigade seems to pay no attention, at least not here; and you substantiate this by the fact that there is a problem in Gornji Vakuf. But before Gornji Vakuf got captured, had you not held any working meetings with the brigade commanders before that, during which it could be stated that, if need be, another brigade could come and strengthen a brigade that needed it? Did such meetings between the brigade commanders not take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 24th, I held a meeting with brigade commanders, and everyone knew exactly what the situation was. Everyone was informed accurately over at the Main Staff as well. The brigade commands had all these documents. I remember that I called a meeting, a quick one, and a very purpose-oriented one, just to make sure they all knew what was going on. That's one thing. The other thing is, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I was the commander of the Main Staff. Even if I had not held this meeting, which I did, it wouldn't have been for the brigade commander to question whether a multiple rocket-launcher should be moved somewhere else or not. If that sort of thing happens, that leaves little room for imagining what else might have happened or how the whole situation worked. It was my right, as a commander, to tell a soldier, Move this multiple rocket-launcher over there. If he refuses to do that, well, then you know what happens in a normal army, and you see what was going on in the HVO at the time. Perhaps I shouldn't say too much, but there were very many lads who fought honorably, many of them were killed. So eventually we managed to put an end to this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a question on this order. Was the Kresimir 4 Brigade directly under your command or was there someone in between, like an operative zone commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an operative zone commander, Colonel Siljeg, but he was the last person they would have listened to or whose orders they would have obeyed. Apart from that, it was my prerequisite to skip certain levels. Obviously, if everything had been working just right, I would have told Siljeg, but I knew with sure and certain knowledge that Siljeg was not a person that they were listening to at all. So I took it upon myself. I did have things my way eventually, but it was very difficult to achieve. You will see in other documents at one point they left their positions and they refused to carry out orders, after which they went on to explain to Vrgoc how they were perfectly within their rights; and, on top of that, that it was well-advised of them to not carry out my order. But you're about to see in an order that will be coming across later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Praljak, you've been telling us for several weeks now that you were surrounded by incapable people, incompetent people. And by way of an example, you are telling us that if Colonel Siljeg had asked for such a rocket-launcher, here he would have not been obeyed. It says if, as a Trial Chamber Judge, I was surrounded by incompetent Judges, I would then seize the President of the Tribunal and say that I cannot continue in this way. When you realised that this situation was like it is, why didn't you turn to President Boban and say, Well, I cannot continue waging the war under these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you talk about a problem of incompetence. I don't think that is a very fortunate turn of phrase. Colonel Siljeg was competent in terms of his military skills. He was fully competent, and he had received military training. Nevertheless, you talk about addressing a presiding judge or a court president. There are two conditions there; no other Judges around, except for the three Judges by your side, and you must try a case, being the second condition. These are the two conditions. I have no replacements for those people, that's the first thing, and the other thing is there's a war going on. If you go to the President of the ICTY, the assumption that you're starting out with is that there are other Judges to go around. And, B, you can actually halt a trial until other Judges are found. But the prerequisites are simply not there in my case. I don't have any replacements. I don't have any other people. Even those I do have were still ten times fewer than the number of men that I would have required to fight like that. And the other thing was I had to go on fighting, waging war, at this point in time. I couldn't just call a stop to the whole thing, Let's set up a judicial system. Let's set up a financial system. And then once all that is done, we can then go on. I simply couldn't do that, and these were the two essential prerequisites that weren't available to me and that you somehow missed out on in your reasoning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for a break. Not yet. All right, well, let's press are on in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, 3D02438. Branko Kvesic was --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interior, the chef de cabinet for the interior. Mr. Stojic was, or perhaps if the situation had been different, he would have been called the minister, chef de cabinet, defence minister, minister of the interior. So not the minister, not quite. He was the chef de cabinet, because that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the number is not right. It's 3D02428. I think that's what it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Shouldn't it be 2438?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2438?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got that interpretation, Your Honour, 2438, 3D, Department for the Interior, Office for National Security, Branko Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's still there. I'm still trying to say, and all the documents confirm this, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, followed by all the documents, say that we are in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then within that, the Croatian Defence Council. The document speaks for itself. According to the establishment links to the National Security Office or through those, Mr. Branko Kresic informs the Defence Department, and then the Defence Department would probably be inform me and Petkovic and Stojic and the Main Staff, in due course, to say that the conditions were now in place for them to meet their promise and liberate Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army, the political and military leaders of the Muslim people, and that they would be heading south towards the sea coast. That wasn't the original idea. Of course, I have no proof for this, but we had found out that this idea was being considered by those persons and was continuing to be considered. There were only a few Croats left in the Neretvica River valley. A single table would be enough to hold them all come Christmastime. That's what it says. It is true that in Bugojno, following the attack that had occurred, but viciously, to be perfectly frank, there had been treason within the town. They were attacked from these joint positions. A large number of shells was used. They took one or two tanks that we had over there, and a host of other weapons, too. And then we were providing more weapons to them throughout, and obviously they were now able to launch an offensive. This also says that they were now getting ready to liberate the right riverbank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, transferring forces means that they were getting forces in from the north and the south and into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02787, please. Thank you. For you, it's 3D02787.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the normal procedure would be, if ammunition was needed in the area, then Colonel Siljeg should be the one submitting a request to the Main Logistics Centre in Grude to Mr. Stojic. Nevertheless, the quick check was run, and one mustn't forget that there was fighting going on all the time. And I found out that there was no ammunition in Grude, whereas there was ammunition in the brigade near Vrgoc. Again, I'm telling him here to dispatch what was required, and I declare him to be responsible in terms of having this order carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is the same Vrgoc as in the previous document; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, can the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D01178, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my document. Within the framework of the Livno Brigade, there was a professional battalion with Commander Vucic at its head. I asked for that professional battalion to go to Rama. And here I'm asking, Where is it, because they were never there, they never came. You will see later on, Ms. Nika, when they came, you will see documents to that effect, they simply refused to join the fray. They went back home with some leisurely stories about why they refused us, about what I had been meaning to dispatch them to. I managed to get Vucic removed when the whole situation calmed down a little bit, and I got another person instead, Mr. Dragan Hinic. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, we have that document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript. We are overlapping and creating trouble for the interpreters. It's pointless. P03971, this is an exhibit. Is this your document? Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Speakers, please do not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people from the Hrvatinic Brigade -- this is from Bugojno, right, the brigade? I think it was from Bugojno; right? Sorry? No, no, I'm not asking -- please, don't mind me. I'm just trying to remember. There is absolutely nothing here that will -- you might ask the question, too, of Mr. Petkovic. He'll be glad to tell you. It's not something that would stand in the way of this trial. Scattered soldiers from Bugojno, some of them, Your Honours, went with other people, crossed Serb-held territory. They had been disarmed there and reached Tomislavgrad eventually, and some went across Rama. There was an attempt, having been previously arrested for a while, to re-establish their units, to have their own commander, and so on and so forth. Nevertheless, they reported to brigades in Tomislavgrad and Livno, Krajl Tomislav and Petar Kresimir [indiscernible]. Some were joining the HOS. There was chaos, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Chaos, a proper chaos. There seems to be a bit of chaos here, too. I see this document, a document indicated 3971. Could it be that you meant "3917"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I'm tempted to say, but I say it with no ill feelings, why didn't you say so in the first time or control the transcript, which would also slow down everybody a little; and, therefore, be a double-purpose measure to assist the proceedings? I'm sorry, I didn't want to offend you at all, but I had to point out. We lose a lot of time. We are lost, and while we are looking for the document, Mr. Praljak is speaking, and -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My mistake. I wasn't watching the transcript to see how the figures were written down. I'll do that in future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, the document speaks for itself. The soldiers who, in different ways, from Bugojno managed to transfer to -- well, a portion of them went to Croatia, and we never saw them again. The other portion stayed in Livno and Tomislavgrad. And with this document what is trying to be achieved is to see to the rest of the brigade and to establish them in military terms, to have them come into Rama and fight, and then perhaps we would be able to go back to Bugojno, from where they were expelled. But they reported to the Livan [phoen] Brigade and Tomislavgrad Brigade and HOS, H-O-S. And, Your Honours, the following also happened there: Some people who were supposed to take up their shifts would pay these others from Bugojno, these men from Bugojno, to go instead of them because the number had to be replenished. And then they would pay 100 or 200 German marks, and then they would go in their place. And this document is an attempt to deal with the situation and to settle this arbitrariness in military terms. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, three brigades are being mentioned here; Kresimir 4th, the Kralj Tomislav Brigade, and then there's the HV Hrvatinic Brigade. What is this Hrvatinic Brigade, HV Hrvatinic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a brigade from Bugojno, and together with the people and the BH Army attack, it disintegrated. So some of those men went across Rama, that is to say Prozor, and reached Tomislavgrad and Livno. Another part of the brigade, together with all the people, didn't manage to flee across Vakuf, but went across Serb territory in Kupres, a mountain there, the Kupreska Vrata. And they were disarmed by the Serbs, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But why is there this HV? Does that mean that it is a brigade from the Croatian Army? Why do we find these two letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means "Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic." And that was a famous historical figure from Bosnia. That was his name. So those are the initials, "HV," "Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, thank you. So nothing to do with the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none, Your Honour. And you can see that from these documents, that they're asking for tanks and soldiers, and that it is absurd to think that I had a brigade of the Croatian Army at my disposal. Well, if you've looked at all the documents, well, I wouldn't have argued over a multiple-barrelled rocket-launcher or anything like that, if there were brigades of the Croatian Army there, a Croatian Army brigade. That's quite absurd. So you'll see the various instances where people were asking for 30 men, 40 men, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now time for a break. It's 10 to 4.00. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Pinter, let's be clear. The Registry told us that you have used 34 hours and 30 minutes so far, and you had initially been granted 36 hours. Does this mean that you are now asking additional time out of your own time, or does it mean that you're going to be finished in an hour and a half's time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or else did you plan to spread your time differently, giving more time to the accused, at the detriment of time for witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I didn't know that there was just two hours left to the end or, rather, an hour and a half. We reached an agreement with General Praljak, and we are going to ask that within the frameworks of our time, total time, that we extend the examination-in-chief of General Praljak and then that the other time will be distributed amongst the witnesses that we plan to bring in. But we shall stay within the frameworks of the time allotted to us by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understood this, but how many more hours will you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until we complete everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As General Praljak has just said, until we get through all the documents that we plan to present. But we were highly selective, and out of a large number of documents, we selected the essential ones, but I -- and I don't expect that we'll surpass the five additional hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if I might ask a question. Do we need to file a motion or make an oral request to over-step the time, or can we consider that we've been given permission to do that by the Trial Chamber as of now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber notes that you will need around five hours. Since you had been given initially 36 hours, and you had one hour and a half left, you will have three -- an additional three hours and thirty minutes. But this time will be taken out, out of the overall time, so it will be deducted from the time that you're going to dedicate for witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wasn't thinking of those five hours, well, counting this one and a half hours. But perhaps we'll be quick, and we'll certainly reduce it at the expense of the witness time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Whatever it may be, any time you may take in addition to 36 hours will be taken out of the 55 hours you had been granted initially.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, would you now open document 3D02066, please. It's an order of yours.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like the VBR, multiple-barrel rocket-launcher, I'm requesting from Mr. Vrgoc to give me, from his stockpile -- well, the stockpiles were at the Main Logistics Base at Grude, but they had been depleted, almost completely exhausted. So I have nothing to add. The brigade, Hrvoje Vucic Kotromanic, is the brigade. No, Hrvatinic, Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic is the name of the brigade. It wasn't from Bugojno but Jajce. I thought about it, and realised I'd made a mistake. It was the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade this other one. So I apologise for that mistake. I misspoke. But the problem is the same, of course. Everything else is correct; that they crossed over Serb territory in their withdrawal and all the rest of it. All the rest of what I said is correct. I just got the names mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now turn to document P03934, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a clear-cut military order. What happened was that the units who arrived in the field had those 15 days, had that fortnight. Then they would ask to be replaced after day 14. And on that territory, there was a lot of fighting going on. And, therefore, it's not possible to replace the troops in that way. And here the order that is being given is that -- well, sets out how troops and units are to be relieved up at the front, and there are many small units with maybe 10 or 11 -- well, they're all very small units. And I've already explained what the situation was like, so I have nothing further to add in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now look at document 3D01195, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the chief of the Main Staff, Brigadier Zarko Tole, who was in the Main Staff and was supposed to be there to deal with the situation in Mostar and Mostar South while I was in Rama and Vakuf, once again is issuing an order saying that there are rules on military discipline, and general rules and regulations for the forces; and that those rules and regulations and orders must be obeyed and carried out; and that once an order arrives, it must be acted upon, because they would go back and ask the Main Staff whether they really meant them to act according to Siljeg's or Lasic's orders or whatever. There was a general mix-up, and then he gives them instructions and says that once an order is given, there's no need for them to go back to the Main Staff, that a military -- that there's a military structure to be followed, and if he received an order from the commander of the operative zone, he has to carry that order out and not to call the Main Staff to ask whether the Main Staff agrees with the order issued by the commander of the operations staff or zone, and that a battalion should ask whether a brigade commander's order is to be respected and carried out or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And it is addressed to the brigades and units, is it, who were -- which were in which area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the area of north-west -- of the north-west, the north-western front, Vakuf-Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Where you were then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Praljak, a technical question. It appears that this order was transmitted by telegram. Can you tell the Chamber whether this was an internal military telegram service, telegraph service, or a generally-functioning service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, there was no telegram service. This was sent in the same way. It's the so-called packet link, packet communication, which was a way of conveying information. And Brigadier Zarko Tole had this device for this packet link or packet connection communication in Grude, and he sent it off to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. There is something that looks like a stamp on the English version, and I do not find anything in the previous version. I don't know how it ever got there, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. This packet communication, there is a stamp saying that this telegram, 5450, was received on the 5th of August at 4.00 p.m. And then there is "RV" that is encircled, and that means radio communication, so this telegram must have been sent by radio; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Packet link is a form of radio communication, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that in the original, we don't have those markings. But since we used Prosecution translations from the Prosecution documents, I'm sure there is a document somewhere with this mark showing that it was sent out by packet communication. But the document is the same, it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Anyway, General, would you now look at 3D02622, please. The date is the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just used the wrong name of the brigade, but it's Eugen Kvaternik, the brigade from Bugojno, and Brigadier Zarko Tole; although this might be General Matic's signature, but that's not essential. Anyway, they're asking that the members of the brigade that had scattered all over the territory should rally together and be sent back to Rama, so everything that I've already talked about and described. He is putting Ivica Primorac -- Colonel Ivica Primorac in charge of this particular assignment, and that anybody refusing to comply should be taken into custody and incarcerated. Now, I don't remember, and I don't know whether Mr. Mate Boban ever, in fact, gave permission or issued instructions for sanctions and methods for punishing disobedience. But I don't remember that we had anything quite -- anything specific. Anyway, the situation I described, about how the people from Bugojno went every which way, how many left for Croatia; I know for sure that the brigade commander, for instance, went to Croatia. He was a psychiatrist, actually, and he went to Croatia, never to return to the territory. He just wasn't interested. He couldn't care anymore. And that he wasn't the only one, but I know about him as a case in point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Now would you take a look at document P03984, please. And the document is the 6th of August, 1993, signed by Zvonko Katovic, and you've already told us something about the way in which the soldiers left the front-line. Could you tell us some more about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the chief of SIS, S-I-S, is reporting here about his line, the line he held, saying what he learnt on the 6th of August, and he goes on to say -- well, the document -- we should read the document. What this is about is as follows: I think that on the 31st of July, going on to the 1st of a August, all the lines around Vakuf fell, and that was some 35 kilometres of military line along which we were attacked. And, Your Honours, this is an event which shows you what can happen in a war. And I remember full well at 2.00 a.m., at 2.00 at night, I arrived at Rama, the forward command post. This was at 2.00 a.m. because I was still touring the positions in Gornji Vakuf, and everything was relatively in order. And then suddenly in the morning, at 6.00 a.m., so after having just slept a few hours, I was informed that all the defence lines in Vakuf had fallen and that all the units, except for some very small ones that were left there, had withdrawn together with the population without anybody having reported about this. So those were situations that you come across in a war, where -- and the operations commander or I, myself -- neither of us were told anything, and then suddenly at 6.00 a.m. in the morning, the road was suddenly full of soldiers and people and cars, a complete jam, and everything had fallen, all the lines had fallen. And I played some kind of role there as you would in a war film, you know, the kind of scenes you saw. I got up on a tank. I walked in the opposite direction. I took up the machine-gun that was positioned on the tank. I ordered some people to follow me, which they did. And then right up until the evening, we managed to regain the same positions that were abandoned the previous night, without anybody asking what had happened or informing us that the lines were down. I saw four or five houses that Croats had set on fire, beautiful houses that people paid for having worked in Germany. They set them on fire, lest they should fall into enemy hands. Such was their attitude, and this tells you how deep the rift already was, mentally speaking. They killed a lot of their own cattle. The houses were not set on fire by the BH Army, but by the owners. I saw some tragic destinies there. A man came back after we stopped the route, and he saw his house burning to the ground, and he had set it on fire, and the cattle dead, the cattle that they had killed. And then he explains -- well, I don't know whether what he says about how he reached it, about how -- whether this knowledge as to how this all came about, how the fall came about, because I didn't have time to investigate. And after all, it was not my job. The SIS was supposed to do that. But, at any rate, I know that all of this fell, and we managed to recapture it.
