But I didn't have time, and I didn't have the capabilities to investigate how it actually came about, apart from this astonishing fact that nobody called me at my forward command post to ask me who and when issued the order to retreat. And, of course, it happened that the ammunition and the whole depot of the Vakuf Brigade had been blown up, and food and the ammunition and the military equipment; so there was a great deal of damage that was caused. But fortunately we did not lose the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was there any rumour -- were there any rumours about Vakuf being sold, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after any political talks, they would -- there would always be those rumours that Posavina had been sold, Bugojno, Jajce. All those who lost their towns would spread rumours that their towns had been sold, that nobody wanted to come to their aid, and that they were left to their own devices. Simply, the air was rife with this kind of misinformation and the endless flow of rumours that all boiled down to some kind of an alibi, because nobody wanted to admit that, Yes, well we were weak, we were not organised enough -- well enough, we did not fight well enough, or the enemy was too strong and we had to give in. Nobody ever admitted anything of the sort. It was always somebody else was to blame, and in most cases this was sold by the politicians as part of some negotiations. But I have to praise myself a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as regards Uskoplje, we managed to actually recapture it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at 3D01146. It's a document that was signed by General Petkovic, and there is another document that is attached to it. It's identical to the first one, but it's more legible, so that you could read it more easily.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing. General Petkovic is a professional soldier, and here in 15 items this is the umpteenth attempt. We had to repeat it over and over again, what needed to be done to improve the overall organisational level of the Croatian Defence Council units, and of course discipline too: discipline, structure, responsibility. So it was repeated endlessly. Orders of this kind, I'm sure there are dozens and dozens of such orders, but this was also repeated orally, endlessly, as to what had to be done, how things should be done, what level of responsibility is required, what kind of conduct was required in war. And I claim that this was a constant -- a constant aspect of all this. It was repeated all over again: begging, pleading, ordering, being angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, at line 17 of page 47, you said that General Petkovic was a professional soldier. In saying so, do you think that he is more or less professional than you are, or are you not drawing any comparison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say a professional, I mean, Your Honours, to say that he had military education. I consider myself to be a professional, too, at the same level as Mr. Petkovic, and I don't feel inferior or superior to him in any way. I think that we are at the same level, but I do grant him the fact that he attended military schools. But we did things in the same way, but what is true is that his orders would look like proper orders as soldiers are taught to draft at school, and I was a bit more lax. But there is no difference in terms of their contents or the meaning or the sense of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at item 10. It is very, very indicative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have an interest in this order, in point 4, where General Petkovic demands that punitive measures be consistently implemented in summary fashion. What is your understanding, what he meant by this? You have spoken about the problem of sanctions before, so I would like to hear what your reaction is when you see this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, this is just a momentary imposition of a punishment. The military could only punish in fraction. Officers of the HVO could punish only in fractions and lack of military discipline. Anything that went beyond that, in terms of punishment, we did not have jurisdiction. If one became aware of it, one had to report it, and then the SIS either learnt of it or had to investigate it, and then an indictment was issued, and then the investigative judge and so on. It was just a judicial procedure then. So I could, in summary proceedings, tell the military police in the brigade, Arrest this man and put him in the brig for 24 hours, or, I don't know, something like that, so, Bring this person into custody. But this was for an infraction, a misdemeanor, but anything about that we did not have jurisdiction, and then it had to -- the security of the town had to deal with it. The military police dealt with the technical side of the issue, to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 10, well, General Petkovic says again, You have to first of all deal with the military aspect, not the civilian aspect. But this does not rule out cooperation with the civilian authorities, but jurisdictions have to be clearly delineated. But these are -- this is just a reflection of our desires, of our wishes that have to be repeated all over again because if you do not repeat them, you will not make any progress in this direction. But the fact that you are progressing slowly, you're progressing slowly because the problem lies with the level of organisation. In other words, the civilian authorities meddled in every single municipality in the military system of command in the military. They would say, Why should the brigade really go to that area or not? So it was a collusion of politics or, rather, the politics influencing the brigade from a town. They were paying their salaries, financing it, and that gave them the right which is not provided for in any law, but they thought they had the right to influence; in some places, to some extent; in other areas, to a great extent or to a lesser extent, but there was always this influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please look at document P04074.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here, apart from the fact that there was a war going on, let me repeat what I've been saying all over again. There are two parallel things. One is solving the problem that had to be solved in any war at that time, at the very moment, that hour, that day, because the military situation demands it; and the other aspect of our work was to improve conditions as much as possible. One of those things is, well, the recruitment, the lads who were old enough to do their national service, pursuant to Mr. Stojic's order, once they completed the order, where they should be assigned, and how they should receive additional training. Because those lads who underwent this brief training, just a couple of months, you couldn't just commit them to combat immediately. You had to assign them to individuals to look after them, in the initial period to initiate them slowly, the way it should be done. And that's how we tried to do it, with some success. And then we would give them to commanders to slowly integrate them into their units, and also they were not supposed to see action in its direst form until they got acclimatised, to a certain extent, to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I have to wait for the transcript. Otherwise, we overlap. So now I would like you to open 3D00802, a document dated the 11th of August, 1993, signed by Emil Harah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is actually relaying an order from the Main Staff, probably dated from the day before, about what should be done in order to improve the quality of the establishment, improving discipline, law and order in the units. Well, I can't really say anything more about this document, apart from saying that as General Petkovic says in his order, this was a continuous task. It was just being repeated all the time. Impose order. Military commanders must do their job properly. Criminal proceedings will be instituted against those who fail to do their job properly. Constant repetition, constantly saying that looting should not be done, that this is a crime, that arbitrary actions are prohibited. I don't have anything else to add to it. It's simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me ask you a difficult question. Since you are under oath and have committed yourself to say the whole truth and nothing but the truth, I'm sure you're going to answer. Look at paragraph number 3 in this document. You can see it. Emil Harah exerts on his subordinates, officers, or blames them for criminal liability in case there were any problems. Do you agree with the contents of this paragraph or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Emil Harah is actually copying the order from the Main Staff. He's just relaying what he had -- he received from the Main Staff, in terms of what he is supposed to do. Of course I agree, because that came from the Main Staff, from me, or from Petkovic. It's immaterial who wrote it, but it came from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you admit that through the entire chain of command from you down to the officer of the unit, if a crime is committed, someone's responsibility is at stake, someone can be incriminated for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's too -- if I say that I agree with you, that's not strong enough. There is not a single person throughout the war. If I knew something, I reported them. It's not a matter of agreeing with something. This must be done. Now, as -- now, there is another question of how this obligation is dissipated in a structure. That's up to you to find out. But I'm telling you under oath that there's not a single detail - we will see from the documents - that I did not fail to report, from people being drunk to looting. I always reported everything, at any time, anywhere, and I demanded that this be a top priority. Now, the group, as a closed set, and the extent -- or the readiness at every level to do that within a group, the group, as a closed set, well, there's a lot of it in literature telling you how difficult that is, and unfortunately we, as the Main Staff or as the military, we didn't have the capability to conduct an investigation. If I learnt about something, then I reported it, but the investigation was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to have a follow-up question to ask from you, Mr. Praljak, and it is the following: If my memory doesn't fail me, I believe that Emil Harah, who was later on put into house arrest or, anyway, he was dismissed, and together with his superior in the municipality. So I wonder if you could tell me what happened to him at a later stage and why. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, I can't say exactly what became of him later on. Nevertheless, you might remember not the order that I wrote but, rather, the letter that I wrote to Mr. Petkovic about Vares, Be merciless, track down some people who can put up with the conditions. That's precisely what happened. There were a number of reports coming from Vares talking about smuggling, indiscipline [as interpreted] and so on and so forth. Given the fact that General Petkovic at the time was in the area, based on a previous agreement, in an attempt to deal with the situation, I wrote him that letter saying, Be merciless, and then the interpretation was "merciless towards the enemy," but that had nothing to do with it. And that was precisely why -- or, rather, why I asked for him to be replaced. Emil Harah surely suffered a mental breakdown at a later stage, based on reports. And he was the one who asked for his own replacement, being no longer in control of the situation and mentally shattered. I don't know what became of him after that, because I, myself, left soon after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have also a little follow-up question, but purely technical. If you don't know the answer, just say so. Disobedience, not obeying an order, is that under military criminal law, as valid in Herceg-Bosna, a criminal offence or is it only a misdemeanor in the disciplinary sphere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a misdemeanor in the disciplinary sphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His Honour asked me. I considered that to be a disciplinary matter. To be perfectly honest, there were times when I couldn't do, simply because then the entire unit said they would leave with that one person, and then I had to find a different way of dealing with that. There was this person that I was supposed to punish, but I had no replacement. And then I would just yell at this person, I would curse this person, and try to find other ways of punishing that person. At this point in time, to impose a disciplinary measure on this person was tantamount to losing the war. There were too many infractions happening all the time. No disciplinary measures would have done, knowing that you had two or three soldiers than required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, were there any court-martials at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were court-martials in military courts. You will come across documents showing that. I think that is one of the following documents. One of the judges talked about the chief of the Main Staff and the extent to which we help them set up, and how many people we reported to them. To be quite frank, military disciplinary courts or whatever, it's not like I was looking to that at the time, not into their names, but there were courts there, some courts. Military, disciplinary, it's hard for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just in order to refer to something else, this is 3D00802, and this document is a result of 3D01146, the previous document that we dealt with, in order to restore order and impose discipline. And now we have 3D00802, which is a result of the behaviour of the brigade commander pursuant to an order from the Main Staff. General, can you please go to 3D01148 [Realtime transcript read in error "3D011148"]?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade Commander Zarko Tole says here that Brigade Commander Milicevic and Colonel Skender were checked and that not a single officer from the staff was present at the command post; although there had been an order that preceded this to the effect that commanders had to be in the thick of the fighting and that there always had to be a duty officer at the staff. We've been through that, too. Your Honours, I wish to tell you that Colonel Skender - and I think he will appear here to testify - is a Croat who served for 33 years in the Legion Etrangere, reaching the highest rank ever granted to a foreigner. He was the commander of a regiment in the Foreign Legion. He'll be here to tell us what he was doing for those 33 years and describe his experiences on the ground to us throughout his career. He was a high-ranking professional of an elite French unit. So what was he to do? He went there to check and found no one. He didn't know what to do, himself. A statement was required to be drawn up and that sort of thing, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02608. The 11th of August, 1993, that is the date.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same thing that we've been talking about. Mr. Zarko Tole, brigadier, quite simply addressing Mr. Morales from SpaBat saying, There, I rejoice. The English took a young girl, Irma, from Sarajevo to London. That caused a worldwide sensation. It was on BBC. It was all over the media for days on end. She had a weak heart. And then he says, We are happy about little Irma being saved. Nevertheless, we had at least 10.000 cases just like this one, saving people and taking them elsewhere. Nevertheless, we were always being closely watched as Balkan criminals. But that was all a matter of power and propaganda. So we see him saying here, Let's not put an end to these steps that we've been taking about our relations. The HVO had approved all of the medical and humanitarian flights across our territory or over our territory. But, unfortunately, our own flights to evacuate our own wounded from Central Bosnia were never approved by the BH Army. We flew, but every time we took off or landed in Central Bosnia, our planes were targeted by the BH Army. All of our aircraft were targeted by shells or other types of artillery fire. They were all pock-marked, our aircraft where. You have the statements made by all the pilots who were involved at the time, and the statements are there for the Chamber to inspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, if I may just state for the purposes of the record that much of what Mr. Praljak has said was his own and not in the document. The reference, for instance, to thousands saved by the Croats is not said in this document. That is Mr. Praljak who says so. I think it is necessary to say so for the record because it could otherwise be misleading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, those are my words. That is something that I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But what about little Irma? This is document based, the fact that she was saved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, page 56, I have been warned that the number was not recorded properly, the document number. It should be 3D01148. The recorded number is one number 1 too many, and I can't quite locate that now. It's page 55, line 12. Thank you very much. It should be 3D01148. Thank you. That's for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can you now please find 3D01229.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my signature, my document. It talks about something that I have told you about already. I approved the plan for a fast-track training of a new generation of recruits to the HVO, and then it goes on to explain this plan, this programme, if you like. It's quite comprehensive. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you now please go to P04207, dated the 15th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P04207.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The date is the 15th of August. In actual fact, if you bear in mind the structure of any normal army, I here address Mate Boban in quite an embarrassing manner. I was adamant that there should be greater involvement on his part throughout the area; not involvement in terms of our differences. That wasn't my job. I wasn't there to meddle in his negotiations and politics. But the negotiations were drawn out, and he was away, and that took some time. And then negotiations kept shifting, so this left a lot of room to the disorganisation of the area. Mr. Boban being away for all those conferences and everything gave rise to certain irregularities and the system meddling in the part of the municipalities. And then I talked to him, and I told him, Well, Grude isn't functioning either, and that's where you are, isn't it? The new shift isn't coming. And then he said he'd do something about that, but the shift never came. And then I went on to ask him -- I was looking for those deserters, and then the report that we submitted for them to be brought in, for them to be escorted in drums [as interpreted] and then brought back to the ranks, but that came to nothing as well. It was all like threatening someone with a rifle that isn't loaded, and the other side doesn't know that the rifle isn't loaded, and then there's a bit of a show-down, one side knowing that the rifle is not loaded and the other not knowing that. But all those committing infractions in one way or another more or less knew that our threats were empty, the verbal equivalent of empty rifles. I will say that we were successful to some degree and people weren't being locked up, you will see from the documents, but unfortunately not sufficiently, or, rather, one couldn't do more than was done. If there was a unit that did not arrive for a replacement, then the unit did not arrive. And after all, based on everything that I know, all the legal systems in all of the world's countries are based on the assumption that no more than a very small percentage of the population will be willing to violate these laws. If you have an amount such as 15 percent of the entire population committing violations, then there is no repression that a country or a state can impose to stop this. It is all too little. The police, the judiciary, neither can do anything about this. And then what happens is a country ends up in a state of chaos, to a greater or lesser degree. These situations in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were dealt with once the war had ended. It was time to draw the line and do something about people who had done something wrong during the war. Efforts were being made and a lot was done, but it still wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Pinter, if I intervene. Mr. Praljak, this again seems to show a rather astonishing lack of organisation and line of command. You are giving an order to the supreme commander of the armed forces and to the president; isn't that so? You say, The mentioned list is to be brought to me within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't agree that I was giving an order, Your Honour. This document was produced following a lively altercation between my own supreme commander and myself. These conversations happened. It's the simple truth of the matter. There was a conversation with no holds barred. I was there as a commander, and I was asking my own supreme commander whether he would start getting more involved about restoring order, regardless of the fact that he was my commander. But we were all human beings, and it was up to us to defend ourselves from a particularly fierce offensive by the BH Army. And then Mate Boban eventually promised me that he would do something about the people in Grude meddling, that he would use his authority -- put his authority at stake to deal with the situation. I was pleading with my supreme commander for assistance. Once I realised that no assistance was forthcoming, then I addressed him with this letter, which you think violated his authority. I don't think that is what it meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is not, in the end, absolutely essential. Another question is: I do not suppose, but maybe I'm wrong, that Mr. Boban, on top or on the side of being the president of the Hrvatska Republika Herceg-Bosna, was also the chief of Grude municipality. And I would have expected that if you want people from Grude, you address those responsible for Grude municipality. Have you done this at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did have a series of conversations and meetings and sharp words to say to the leadership, but not with Grude. I asked Mate Boban here, because he had his office in Grude and that's where he was born. He was born nearby, and he wields a certain amount of authority. He has clout over there, as he does in -- I don't know what his authority is in other parts, but Grude is his hometown, so I asked him to put some order into that place, Grude. And can I add something else, Judge Trechsel? Whether a place was well ordered or not, well, they would put some order into the situation, and then there would be a dispute, and then there would be a lot of disorder. So the curve would go up and down, but mostly it depended on whether they had managed to find a good commander or not. Now, a good commander was either somebody who was very prominent in the area, and it was difficult to find such people because there were always some groups that were opposed, but if you brought in somebody from outside, that is to say, somebody who was from that place and then went to the Croatian Army and spent the war there and was promoted in his career, if you managed -- and he was an honourable person, if you managed to bring him in as a commander, and that kind of commander, then he would put some order into a unit. So we had 11 replaced commanders. For example, in the Rama Brigade, we went through 11 commanders, replacing them one by one, around August and September, until a man called Pavlovic arrived. And he was able to put some order into things. But it depended on many factors of which I don't have time to go into here to bring home all the complicated factors and complex situation that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we have the feeling that you asked Mate Boban to make sure that law and order was being restored, whereas he might have believed that it was for you to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I always wonder, and I keep asking myself, Well, just tell me how? All I want to know is: You say at that point in time, Praljak, you're not there, but I am envisaging a person B from the French Army. And he could introduce law and order; whereas it's your fault, Praljak, that there isn't any law and order there. So if somebody were to explain to me how, I would write any -- sign any chit for punishment. For example, I went there. I went to a meeting. But they didn't want to, they didn't want to listen. And it's up to me you say, Your Honour, up to me. I know what my duty is, but all I have to see is how I'm going to implement that duty of mine. How can I make it work? And I expect you to write, at the end of all these proceedings of this trial, I would expect you to write, Praljak, if I were in your place, I would do it that way, if you just imagine a French general, or an English general, or whoever. But you know what I'm like. I know how to shout, I know how to swear. I know how to beg, how to threaten. I'm strong. I know how to do this and that. You know the kind of man I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you this question because I remember a document -- I don't remember the number of the document. I apologise for not giving you the number of this document, since we review thousands of documents. I have a good memory, but as far as this document is concerned, I can't give you the number of it. But this document stemmed from the military police, and this document stated that Tuta's men are indulging in ethnic cleansing. I assume that this document, stemming from the military police, must have been forwarded up the entire line and then something must happen. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I don't know that a document of that kind went up and down the hierarchy. That's the first point. And the second point is that I don't know what the military police could have done to Mr. Naletilic at that point in time, except to commit another crime; and that is to shoot without a trial. As far as I know, and I know from my own experience as I've recounted it to you, you weren't able to deal with a situation on the basis of law and lawfully. You could only do it by shooting, and that, again, is quite another story, quite another kettle of fish. So there were groups that you couldn't control in any other way except to enter into a mutual war outside any legal control, and then that's debatable, would anybody enter into a war like that. And, secondly, this would bring us to a situation of complete anarchy, with everybody doing what they thought should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to insist on this now, but I shall revisit the issue later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, did you receive military police reports regularly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we did not receive military police reports regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now a correction to the transcript. On page 60, line 21 -- I'll ask you the question, but I'd just like to put that right in the transcript. You said that there was a meeting and that you held a meeting with the leadership, the leadership, all the politicians of the HZ-HB, or just with certain leadership in a certain town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In response to Judge Trechsel's question, or whoever asked me about why I didn't talk to the municipality officials, and I quoted the example of Ljubuski, when a whole brigade refused to take up their positions up at the lines. And their reason was a very banal one, that is to say, that somebody had employed somebody in the Customs office and so on. And they said that until that situation was solved, we wouldn't go to war. So that was what that was all about. And I remember that at a meeting there, there was Mr. Stojic, and he couldn't do anything either, and then I -- although it wasn't a time when I was officially performing my duties in the HVO. Anyway, I asked that people from the village who were party members should come forward, people who were well known, and we would resolve the situation as it is resolved at some pre-electoral campaign, for example, by trying to persuade them; they would put forward their demands, saying the situation had to be resolved; they asked to become members of the municipal council, although they weren't elected; then I asked that municipal council to take in a certain number of members because otherwise they wouldn't go up to the front and the lines. The entire brigade refused, so we couldn't set up any kind of structure beyond what we had to deal with. The brigade simply didn't want to take up its positions, and that was the end of it. Now, Judge Antonetti was asking me what my duty was. My duty was to prevail upon the brigade to take up their positions at the lines, and the brigade didn't want to do that. So what could you do, faced with a situation like that? I told you what I did, and I maintain that nobody could have done a better job. You couldn't do otherwise, for the simple reason that -- well, I'm not an idiot. The easiest thing would be, of course, for the brigade to take up their positions. But if the brigade didn't want to take up its positions, then you have to resort to other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you know that I presided over another trial. I can say this because it was in open session. It looks as though the BH Army also encountered problems within its own brigades. And at some point in time, they decided to take action against a specific reluctant brigade, and there was a major-scale operation. Now, if there were any problems within the HVO, why was nothing done against the culprits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Judge Antonetti, it's not true that nothing was done. A lot was done. Secondly, you assume that it involved small numbers and that when you eliminate these small numbers, you would have law and order. But that's not correct. It's not just a few people. It's not only three commanders. The brigade commanders did want to take up their positions, but the brigade, the men, didn't want to. And there were several hundred people there who didn't want to take up their positions. So you'd have to take up action against several hundred people, which is something that you can't do, Judge Antonetti, and those would be the military requirements. Of course, in another army, this would be tantamount to rebellion. However, here it was a fact that you had to deal with and face. And on the assumption that you did have the power and authority to put 300 soldiers in prison, into some kind of prison, you still wouldn't have another 300 soldiers to take up their positions at the front-lines. So it wasn't a problem that could be solved within the frameworks of the resources that you had and the way in which we acted and in which we existed. And that's what I claim, because that was the situation that I was in, that I faced, and I'd like to know what it is that I should have done or what should have been done. Of course, the BH Army, Your Honours, faced the same sorts of problems, and I'll tell you why some problems they found easier to solve, disciplinary-wise. That is to say, they linked certain activities and discipline with the distribution of humanitarian aid. That is to say, if a soldier was disobedient, they would withhold humanitarian aid to that person's family. And we didn't have the possibility of doing that in Herzegovina because, quite simply, we weren't able to control the humanitarian aid coming in. We were closed off, and everybody would go off to Croatia whenever they wanted to, at least those who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'll put to you something which you will consider as provocative, probably. And it's not at all my intention to provoke, but I think in sheer honesty I have to tell you. Listening to you this afternoon, I start wondering whether this war, that is presented as a war of the Croatian Narod for their popular rights, these people's rights, in fact, is not something that the people wanted, but that a small stratum, a class, a caste of politicians and military and other very nationalistic-minded people wanted, and which they then whipped through, not being pushed from underneath, from the popular, from the grassroots; but, on the contrary, pulling out the grass to throw it into the war, to some extent. What is your reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that question, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour. First of all, I don't consider that there are any provocative questions. I don't experience any questions as being provocative. And I'm ready to answer any question you wish to ask me, and I've repeated umpteen times that nonetheless a large number of people did man their positions up at the lines. But I'm talking about the problems that occurred here, and because I am talking and addressing the problems, I don't mean to say that this applied to everybody. The Ljubuski Brigade, for example, which at one point for some reason or other -- or, rather, one unit didn't want to man the lines, but it was a fantastic brigade. And when they went back to Vakuf after losing their units, their men first followed me. There wasn't any nationalism there, nationalistic feelings outside what we considered to be national feelings, and that is that they were supposed to fight anybody attacking them in the places where they lived. Now, we could not assume that any individual in Herceg-Bosna, for example, could force somebody to go and fight. If it was only Mate Boban and Slobodan Praljak who had wishes of that kind, then the whole population would have left and gone to Croatia. Nobody would have stayed on to fight because you couldn't find anybody to fight. And I'm talking about 80 to 90 percent of the population, with a lot of casualties and suffering, fought very valiantly and bravely and honestly and honorably. But of course you had the problems, and those are things that I'm addressing, and you couldn't apply this model to everyone. And that is why those who fought were volunteers. They fought because they wanted to fight. And I keep stressing that. Those who wanted to go there came and went because they wanted to. It was their wish to go. Had they not wished to go, there was no force that could have made them or no laws. Laws did exist, but there was nothing you could use to prevail upon them, because Mr. Buntic or whoever could write down a law very quickly. But to ensure that the law was implemented and acted upon, well, I'd like to hear from you how that would be possible. I told you how I implemented the law, with the disarmament of those in Dretelj and so on: might fighting might, pistol versus pistol, weapons against weapons. I didn't do anything because I liked doing things like that, Judge Trechsel, but because that was the only way to act, given the situation, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I just note that, on the other hand, if it was only 10 or 20 percent that caused problems, I find it less persuasive that it was not possible to contain that minority in some way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 percent is a great deal. Five percent is a lot, especially, if you will allow me to tell you this -- well, you know, it's not always the minority that's the problem, but it is the silence of the majority that is the problem. The problem of Nazi-ism in Germany wasn't so much the problem of the Nazi Party in 1933, but it was the silence of the majority that allowed them to develop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I'll end it with this: Hitler was elected with a majority, unfortunately. But please, Ms. Pinter. We are leaving the terrain of the indictment; I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say, Hitler, when he was elected, promoted a completely different political programme than the one he actually realised and put into practice. But be that as it may.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the Main Staff, was it responsible for the situation in the rear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn to document P04235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. General, your lawyer asked a question: Was the Main Staff responsible for the situation in the rear? And you answered, "No." I am flabbergasted. Why do you say "no" to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because it isn't so. Somebody should have placed the units at my disposal, whoever is competent for that, the mobilisation departments in the municipalities. And once the units were mobilised in the municipalities, they were supposed to be equipped by the Defence Department, they were supposed to be issued with uniforms and other stuff, and then the Main Staff was supposed to get this unit equipped in this manner for its use. The Main Staff had nothing to do with the rear, except in cases where somebody is trying to resolve some problems using private channels, as we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take a metaphor from the theatre world to illustrate my thought. Imagine that a director wants to put a play on stage and he's looking for actors for the play, but he fails to find any. Therefore, the director is never going to put this day the play on stage; do you agree with that? Now, try to apply this metaphor to the army. There are problems, but no men, no logistics, no doctors, no courts. Do you have to wage war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in theatre it's a little bit different, but I don't think that you're entirely in the right. You can direct, I don't know, Shakespeare's "Hamlet," with a large number, with a large cast, or you can do an abridged version and eliminate some of the roles and give one actor several roles. So the same goes for Don Juan, depending on that, and it is not always right that the best theatre is born out of conditions where you have everything. Sometimes the narrowness and lack and shortage of some things produces the best performances. Secondly, as regards the army, everything that you said is right. There were problems everywhere, in every aspect. But day after day, Judge Antonetti, you have in the field only two options; to issue an order to retreat, and -- or in the face of all the shortcomings, you say, I remain here and I will do everything I can at this point in time, in those circumstances, for this period with my energy, with my brains, my knowledge, to prevent the situation from deteriorating. That's your choice. The choice is there, at that point in time, in that place. And if you recall, when I put the pistol next to Mr. Buntic's head because he claimed years before that, as a friend, that he would fight, and then your typical intellectual, the people who I call peace profiteers, because there are war profiteers in war, but there are thousands and thousands of intellectuals who are peace profiteers. These are the people who say, Well, there's something horrible going on there. And then they trot around the various capitals of the world, sipping champagne and explaining how peace should come about, and they have been doing that for thousands of years. Well, they simply withdraw and they said, Well, Praljak could -- I could have gone to Germany. I had a resident permit, a work permit there. I could take care of my family there, and let other people wage war. I stayed, and I would have stayed again because every day I had this choice. And I always stayed. I was convinced -- completely convinced that my remaining there means that the situation would be at least a millimetre better than it would be without me. And I made this improvement by 1 millimetre, and this is what I'm testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are 10 minutes left before the break, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you whether the Main Staff had the obligation to maintain law and order in the rear.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How? How was it supposed to? With what?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like you to turn to document P04235 [Realtime transcript read in error "P04325"].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already seen this document. The date is the 16th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. The number has not been recorded properly. P04235. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So at this point in time, I, as the commander of the Main Staff, demanded reports on how many troops do we have in the theatre; not how many people are in the records, but how many people are there actually fighting. And then when I carried out my own order, I actually sent this report to myself, to the Main Staff, for this section of the battle-field. And I say that there are 21 units on this section of the front-line. Look at the figures here, and I say that it's a total of 4.424 soldiers on paper. They're all in some files somewhere, in some records. But more than a half are not there. More than a half are just not there. And now again we have the same question, Should I stay or should I go? Well, we stayed there, and we succeeded. And we succeeded because the other side was no better. If the HVO of this kind, brave lads, fought well, if a regiment of the Foreign Legion or an elite unit of the Marines faced us, we would have lost the war. But the people on the other side were worse than we were, and that is why they failed to defeat us. Let me be frank and clear. And in despair before the situation, I say this: Well, fuck this, because this phrase, it just explains to you, it tells you, well, that's how it is, there's nothing I can do, because if the people from Sebesic, who had been expelled from their area, they are all mentally ill. They are exhausted. They are already decompensating. Their health has deteriorated. They used to be students, farmers, craftsmen, and they were thrown into this bloody war. They were expelled from their territory. They don't know where their families are. They don't know what is happening. These people were sick in their heads, and it is much more important to them to hear somebody speak to them and somebody run from one trench to another than to have the system of command and control as it was in -- as it exists in normal armies. I kept them alive. I kept them fighting, simply because 90 percent of my waking hours were spent with one unit, another unit, the 15th unit, in the trenches, fighting side by side with them. And that's simply how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The 5th Guards Brigade --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'll probably be speaking about that later on. The 5th Guards Brigade is the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army from Vinkovci. And I've explained this, and let me repeat. Those people who were around Vukovar and Vinkovci, they were people from Herzegovina who had settled there in the 1950s, in the 20th century, in the properties or farmsteads of the Volksdeutscher, who had been killed or expelled from the former Yugoslavia. And there were more than 550.000 of them, the ethnic Germans. They, themselves, and their children still kept ties with their original home, Herzegovina. And from that brigade, I managed to get 130 infantrymen who were, for the most part, from Herzegovina. They were volunteers. And they volunteered to fighter there because they had this -- some kind of a feeling towards their home because they all had old houses there and their grandparents, so they were volunteers. This is proof that the Croatian Army did not have a presence there, because otherwise I would have gotten a brigade from Imotski, from Split, or from Sibenik because they were all stationed close by. Those were volunteers from the 5th Guards Brigade, the descendants of the Herzegovinians who had been moved from Herzegovina and settled in the homesteads of the ethnic Germans who had been expelled. And that's why they volunteered to fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the record, and it's been suggested that I should ask you what Volksdeutscher or ethnic Germans are.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volksdeutscher, Maria-Theresa, at the time when she ruled, the empty sways of land - I don't have a map - so north of the Danube and in the Banat region, that is northern parts of Serbia and eastern parts of Croatia [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbia"], Germans were settled there. And they lived there for two centuries. They were citizens of Yugoslavia. They were locals, domestic population. But after the end of World War II, some of the Volksdeutscher retreated with the Wermacht, the German Army. A large number were taken by Russians into exile, to Russia. And they worked, and some of them survived after 20 or 30 years, and a large number ended up in the camps in Yugoslavia. And I explained all that in the book that I submitted to the Trial Chamber. Now, the Volksdeutscher, they were the richest part of this population, with the biggest farms and properties. They were all empty now, abandoned. And in the 1950s, people from the poorest areas in Yugoslavia - Montenegro, Herzegovina and so on - were put on trains and driven up there, because it was rich soil. They were taken there to till the land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when one looks at this document, one has to draw a parallel with the forces of the other warring parties. Here we can see, when it comes to Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, we have 4.424 fighters, but when you see the lazy ones, those on leaves, the ill men, then the figures is drastically reduced. And then we see there are some units who are only scores of men strong. On the other hand, we have had documents speaking about artillery, rocket-launchers, helicopters, aircraft, the VRS, 130.000 men in the 3rd Corps. So one is bound to ask oneself what kind of war the HVO was waging. Were they tiny, local conflicts with a handful of men each time? Or was it a conflict such as the conflicts we could see during World War II, with thousands of men? With the figures you show, the impression is rather that we are speaking about tiny or limited conflicts. And earlier on you said, In spite of it all, we won. So explain to me, where did you win?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, this has nothing to do with World War II. In World War II, and I've shown you this, a division -- at least 12 to 14.000 people holds a line 7 or 8 or 10 kilometres, if you are defending. This has nothing to do with it. So the French divisions that fought the Germans held at most 10 kilometres of the defence lines. So between this and World War II, there is no comparison, generally speaking. On the other side, the ratio was maybe 1:5, 1:6, so the BH Army in this area was attacking us with this balance of powers. That's number 2. Number 3, those people who stayed to fight were brave lads, headed by me. We were brave lads. We fought well. Some people got killed, but we were ready to fight well. And, thirdly, when I say we won, I mean we did not lose. And they did not achieve their strategic objective, which was to reach their western borders and to reach the sea. So I did not issue any orders for attack. There are only orders to defend ourselves. And here in Mostar, in Vrdi, and in the south, we defended ourselves. And when I say "defended ourselves," by that, I mean we won. And that is why I remained there in spite of everything lest we should lose. And that meant that we won. Because even when we fought Serbs, we didn't go towards the Drina, to Nevesinje, to defeat the Serbs. We did not fight to defeat the Serbs. We fought not to lose or to prevent them from implementing their objective, which was to achieve a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll resume after the break at 10 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I ask another question about a document, there is something I'd like to say about page 74 of the transcript. The line number is 6. It reads that the general said that the Germans were settled in Eastern Serbia, whereas it should have read "Eastern Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now P04260, please. That's your order dated the 17th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So whether on the same day or the day before, the day before -- so on the 13th of August, a large-scale attack of the BH Army on South Mostar occurred, the 13th, the 14th, the 15th and so on and so forth. I was involved in the fighting, and we managed to take back most of the positions that we had lost. There was one remaining, a minor hill, that we took back at a later stage. Some prisoners were being taken to the front-line. There is prior inform about that from Zarko Tole, the head of the Main Staff. Based on his information, and I was on my way to Rama when I found out, I issued an order for all the prisoners to be withdrawn from these labour tasks they were performing. And I also said that I should be kept up to date. But I hadn't had any previous information from anyone at all indicating that anyone was doing anything like that, taking these prisoners to the front-line to dig trenches, something that was entirely forbidden. A day or two after my return to the Main Staff, I issued this self-same order to everyone. I don't have the order, regrettably, but there was a witness here who talked about that order that came at the time from the Main Staff. One thing that I found surprising about this is the fact that I was somewhere along the front-lines. And the thing that strikes me as incredible is that I never saw this happen myself, prisoners digging trenches. I proposed to the OTP to try and track down something like that. I would have been identified. That much is certain. I'm certain that if I'd been there, some prisoners would have identified me because of some of my physical features. I never, ever saw prisoners dig trenches. And you can't say that I wasn't spending time along the front-lines. This was entirely surprising to me. I issued the order that I issued. And afterwards, I received feedback, a report saying that this was complied with, and that the prisoners were back in prison, and that the persons responsible were the persons responsible; the wardens. And a carbon copy was submitted also to the military police and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you were on the front-line, I assume you had binoculars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your binoculars, were you watching the opposite side and were you overseeing what they might be doing there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, to the extent that we could. But one was able to observe, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you realise, whether it was on the Serb or the Muslim side, that they sometimes used prisoners for construction work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw that happen, Your Honour, on any of the sides. I am slightly thrown by this. If you look at witness evidence, you will realise that the situation was what it was. I was constantly moving from one front-line to another, and I am still surprised to this very day. I never saw a single man perform a task like this. I never came across that, because I certainly would have treated those commanders who would have been in charge of something like that differently. I do propose, however, to the gentlemen from the OTP to track down a single witness who saw me there and who was performing labour there. There had to be someone who could identify me then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get back to this later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the Presiding Judge said whether these prisoners were used for digging purposes or fortification purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript, page 77, line 24, when the general was speaking about who would have been responsible for taking people to perform labour, and then he mentioned wardens, prison wardens, and also guards; whereas the word there in the transcript is "brigades." Could the general please explain what he said, because this might lead to some confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigades, the HVO, had no authority whatsoever over the prisons, the army over the prisons, none. Frankly speaking, I don't know who it was that did have power over the prisons. I know that we had no power over the prisons. I don't know what the legal position was in relation to this element of the military police. I never went into that. But neither the brigade, nor the operation zone, nor the Main Staff, had anything to do with the prisons. The only thing we did was send to these prisons the persons that we previously punished.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pinter. I think this is an important point that needs to be clarified as much as possible. If I understood you correctly, Witness, you have now stated that on or around the 15th of August, 1993, you became aware of the fact that prisoners were engaged in work such as digging trenches. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I said that on the 13th, 14th and 15th, there was large-scale fighting in the south of Mostar, and that was something that I was involved in myself. On this day, or the day before, the 17th or the 16th of August, word reached me from Zarko Tole, the head of the Main Staff, saying that he had received information indicating there were prisoners being taken to perform labour and dig trenches. It was based on his information, and I was in the operations area, that I issued this order. Immediately afterwards, however, I issued an order to all strictly prohibiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information on what kind of prisoners were engaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that the only reason to immediately forbid this would be the fact that if prisoners of war are so engaged, that would be a crime, a war crime. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now I'm interested to hear from you what you did to prosecute those responsible for that crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, aside from this order, which said that this must not be continued, I did nothing. The simple reason being, this was submitted to the SIS, and they knew about this. I had no means of conducting an investigation, since I had received no reports from any quarters. The Main Staff simply doesn't have the operative potential required to conduct an investigation. If I received no report about anything whatsoever, then it would have been up to the SIS because they were the military body in charge of investigations. That was their job description. And then if information is received, there is a certain procedure that follows, and that is up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who, according to you, would bear the responsibility for prisoners being engaged in such work as digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever did that, they didn't ask for approval. Based on what I have seen here so far, frankly, aside from this information and the ban that applied at the time, I had no other information on that. It was here, during this trial, that I realised that some people went there and that some people issued approvals. This is certainly a crime, and I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. To be a bit leading, would you agree that it is the military commander who assigns the work to the prisoners, perhaps alongside the military police? I leave that aside. But isn't the military commander also at least criminally responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military commander cannot determine what the prisoners will do. I don't know how a military commander should be responsible, unless he had not issued an approval, unless he had no knowledge of this going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Some military commander has placed an order for prisoners to be put at his disposal. And we have, in this courtroom, seen hundreds of such requests. These people were immediate authors of that war crime. I would suggest prima vista, without going into details of mens rea and so forth. Now, would it not be, or is it not the duty under international law for the commanders and the commanders of the commanders to react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, without going into legal matters, no commander is allowed to take prisoners of any kind at all and use them to dig trenches along the front-line. In the Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia, and as I went about writing all those booklets and all, I knew full well under what conditions and for what types of work prisoners of war could be used outside a theatre of war. Within the prison compound, where they were, they could perform some tasks there. Not just POWs, but also ordinary prisoners, they could help with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's kind of you to tell us what the 2nd Geneva Convention says, but I don't think that it is really called for. Thank you. Thank you for your answer. Excuse me, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if we had standing before us the military prosecutor, and we could have had him standing in front of us if the Prosecutor had called this person. And the military prosecutor, according to the documents in question, would have said this: I have been seized when the SIS or the military police files a report, and then I seize the investigating judge. This is what a military Prosecutor would say. But I would then say to the military prosecutor, If the SIS and the military police don't seize you of this, what would he say? He would turn around and say, I don't do anything because I don't know anything about it. Based on this suggestion, what you are saying has been confirmed in the document. You have told the SIS and you told the military police that from 6.00 p.m. onwards, there should be no prisoners. Fine. But if we had standing before us the man in charge of the SIS, he would say to us that he had received no orders from Mr. Praljak and that he didn't do anything about it. Therefore, if we had the head of the military police, this person would say to us, I didn't receive an order; therefore, we didn't do anything. So we found ourselves in a system where the military prosecutor says that he has not been seized of this fact, the SIS states that it received no order, the military police states that it received no order, and you say, I haven't done anything. Don't we have a problem here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, there is no problem whatsoever. I am in no position to issue any orders to the SIS, nor did I have a need, or indeed to the military police. They do this in their line of duty, like the local police here in The Hague do, or anywhere else. It's in their job description. They have to do this. It's their job. They don't need anything. They're not under my command. I don't need anyone issuing orders to me for me to say this brigade or this unit should go there or go elsewhere, that's where we'll be fighting, and so on and so forth. It is my duty to exercise control over the soldiers to the extent that I can, successfully or poorly, with more success or less success. But I don't expect that I should be given daily orders about this. Likewise, the SIS have their rules, and these rules say in a battalion or in a brigade, it's right there. And because it's their job, they gather intelligence, and then they act upon this intelligence. They have the power to bring people in. They have a badge, they have ID to bring people in. They can call in the military police to study some technical circumstances surrounding a murder or anything like that. It's their job. Your job is to try cases. It's not like you need to go to someone every day to tell you that you are a judge, Your Honour. It's what you do. I have no power to issue orders to the military police or the SIS. They are separate departments, and I explained why it was done the way it was; in order not to have too much power accumulating under a single commander. And this is the established practice in other democratic countries, especially those that don't keep large-scale professional military forces. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at the reactions to this order of yours, and that is P04285, the next document. The date is the 18th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Here we have commander Ante Pavlovic informing on the fact that all the soldiers were sent back. They were withdrawn pursuant to that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now let's move on to the next document, which is 3D02063, and the date is the 21st of August, 1993. Is that your document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature, and once again this is on the subject of the Croatian Army. And here I'm informing the 4th Brigade of the HV Split, that's the Guards Brigade, that their member Franjo Lucic, who was on leave, he was off duty and remained on the theatre of operations in Gornji Vakuf. He was obviously originally from Bugojno. And I'm asking that this absence be justified and not to proclaim him a deserter; to certify his absence. He says he wants to stay on there. So this is a document showing my relations with the army and Gojko Susak and so on, and I have to issue a certificate to excuse him from his absence from the 4th Brigade; whereas, in fact, it is said that I disposed of brigades of the Croatian Army. So let me repeat, once again, that is just not true, not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, which is 3D02087, and it's a document dated the 23rd of August, 1993. And the ATG, and the signatory is Slobodan Praljak. So it's one of your documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what's been added there in handwritten form?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it says. But once again, well, when it says "ATG," anti-terrorist group, I would like to say, Ms. Nika, that it was a matter of 25 soldiers, whereas only 7 of them were in Prozor. The rest were visiting family or on a leave of absence. So this is just to show the forces we had and the small units that we had. And we had to contend with the situation there with those few men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Pinter. I only would like to come back for one moment to the previous document, that is, which was the 3D02063. And, of course, Mr. Praljak has already explained that there was a certain Vlado Lucic from Bugojno, and he remained in the battleground in Gornji Vakuf. And, therefore, they should excuse him from the brigade until further notice. And here there is a reference to the HV, Croatian Army 4th Brigade, et cetera. Now, what Mr. Praljak explained before, that it shows that there was no direct involvement of the Croatian Army in that particular region; that is, in Herceg-Bosna, in Herzegovina. On the other hand, I found it a bit strange that -- and because of the major assumption is that all those who were from the HV, that is, the Croatian Army, they are supposed to be volunteers. In front of this situation, my question is to

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK THAT
utterances.text: Why should they have notified the Croatian Army that a certain person was there and who, in a way, fought there in the battleground in Gornji Vakuf? So my question is related to the fact that there was a certain flow of information between the HVO and the HV. If my assumption is correct, what would you say, Mr. Praljak? Was there a kind of constant flow of information there and vice versa between the two military establishments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a very weak flow of information, and you'll see from some other documents I'm either requesting something or writing a piece of information of this kind. Obviously, I know the gentleman. He arrived from Split, from Dracevac, in actual fact, which is where that brigade was stationed, to visit his parents who were expelled from Bugojno. I remember him. And then I said, Listen, stay here, help us out, because he was an experienced fighter from the Croatian Army. I asked him to stay there and to fight with us, and he said, All right, fine, but you have to write to my brigade, because if I don't report for duty after my leave of absence, they will write out a warrant. It's the Guard Brigade, a professional brigade of the Croatian Army. And there was far more law and order there, and they would have issued a warrant for his apprehension. So he's asking me to write and say that he stayed on as a volunteer so that they wouldn't pursue him. And I'm saying that, Judge Prandler, because if we're dealing with only one man from the Croatian Army here where -- that if he had two or three brigades at his disposal, he wouldn't have -- it wouldn't have mattered. He would have told this one man to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the next document, 3D01732, is what I would like us to look at. It is dated the 24th of August, 1993, and it was written by the Command of the 111th XP Brigade at Zepce? Can you remember today, here and now, what situation Zepce was in, in August 1993; and what could have been the reasons for this document having been written?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zepce was in a total encirclement, under siege. And it was attacked by the BH Army as one of the pockets where the HVO managed to stay put and not be expelled as it had been in Konjic and in other parts. Now, I don't have anything to add to this letter. It speaks for itself. It was sent to Boban and Prlic and Stojic and the Main Staff, and the commander in Vitez to whom they belonged previously as the operative zone, operations zone. And here it's not the commander signing, himself, but the Command, so all the people over there. They're wondering what the policy being waged is and what the object is. And they describe how the aggression started, when it started, and so on and so forth. So I have nothing to add to this document, except to say that it is one of a series of documents which arrived from Zepce, and Vares, and Busovaca, and Vitez, and all the rest of it, the operation zone, and what situation they found themselves in under aggression from the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I think the only important and relevant thing is how it all began, how the aggression began, and when it began.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: With an attack on --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica, when the full, complete blockade of Zepce was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at the next document, which is 3D00800.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Emil Harah reporting, saying that on the 26th of August, the attack began in Kopjari. And it is the same place, Kopjari, where two months later the BH Army attacked Vares. And he says here that they have five wounded and foresees that a clash with the BH Army is imminent, and that one should have no illusions. Everyone, the civilian authorities, the military authorities, all the soldiers, and everyone else, knew that the conduct of the BH Army was such that, well, from the end of March and beginning of April, 1993, that it only had one objective, and that was to defeat the HVO and to expel the Croats and the HVO from those territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. May we now look at the next document, which is 3D00639. It is the 28th of August, 1993, the civilian population leaving the war zone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of my documents. I signed it. And it refers to a very narrow area at Pidris, the area near Mackovac, near Gornji Vakuf. You see that on the left. And because of the exceptionally strong attack -- well, the attacks were already going on, but especially when the artillery came into play, then there was a strong attack. And I ordered that the civilian population be moved out of those two small pockets where fighting was going on. And that is the villages of Pidris and Mackovac. Because, well, I think that there was some civilian casualties, and I didn't want to allow the civilians to be involved in any fighting. So I asked that the women, children, and elderly men who were not fit for military service be moved out, that we should find somewhere to send them to, and except for the civilians who were soldiers or auxiliary workers, workers helping out those who were transporting things, loading, unloading trucks and so on, helping in some ancillary way; anyway, I'm telling the Judges here and you, Ms. Pinter, I'm saying in point 3 that they should take their livestock with them so that the cattle was also moved out, so that they have something to live on. They can milk the cows and so on. So that's something I also say. I considered this to be quite normal and necessary and logical. And I think that legally it was in order too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you tell the Chamber whether the population of these two villages was mainly or exclusively Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, as far as I remember, there were Muslims, too. But I didn't really pay attention to these ethnic matters. I asked that everybody be dealt with in the same way, according to the same principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small misunderstanding with respect to the transcript, but everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now please look at document 3D02062, and this, judging by the signature, is your document. The date is, once again, the 28th of August, 1993. And it is an order, one of your orders.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once again to Petar Kresimir the 4th, and it speaks for itself, everything is quite clear. All one needs to do is to read what I wrote down additionally. And it says only an idiot can send people into the field just like that, without any logic, without any communications. So this man sent the men he sent in the way he sent them. And they had no means of communication. So I say he's an idiot. That's all I could say, that he was an idiot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02448 is the next document I'd like us to look at. Your signature is not on that document, but are you the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, well, this document is clear and speaks for itself. I'm asking for 30 men for three days, from the 28th of August to the 31st of August, not even 3 days. And I'm asking for 30 men to cover some void until I make other arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's move on to the next document, which is 3D001100, and it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's just one 0.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D01100. Yes, that's right. And there's no date.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in this document, 3D02418, the addressees are the commander of the Rama Brigade and also again the commander of the HV Kotromanic. What is this HV Kotromanic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic is the name. He was a nobleman from medieval history, Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic, the brigade from Jajce. And in Jajce was -- Jajce was the seat of the Bosnian Croats Catholics' kings. One of them was Hrvoje Vucic Hrvatinic. And there was a lovely painting that we would see in our textbooks at school where he would be mounted on a horse in all his splendor. Anyway, this is not the HV, Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the record, there was a mistake in the English version in the translation because it is written "Kotromanic," whilst in the B/C/S version we find the name that you have just indicated, Hrvatinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
